newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast agrees cocoa reform - donor source.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast agrees cocoa reform - donor source.

text.p: Ivory Coast has reached an agreement with donors on liberalising cocoa marketing for its 1999/2000 season, a donor source said on Monday.

"They have agreed to liberalise cocoa from October 1, 1999," said the source, although he added that one week of talks with the Ivory Coast had failed to result in a wider agreement on a new Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.

"There will be no bareme (government list of marketing prices) and no indicative minimum reference prices," said the source. Ivory Coast's Caistab commodities board, which had a monopoly on cocoa and coffee marketing until 1995, would also be reformed.
"For the moment we are calling it restructuring," said the source.
Ivory Coast has loosened its monopoly on cocoa and coffee marketing since 1995 under the terms of a $150 million agriculture credit from the World Bank -- which has since pushed for further changes.
Donors and Ivory Coast earlier this year agreed in principle to sweeping coffee liberalisation reforms from 1998/99, but negotiations on cocoa had proceeded more slowly.
Under the new agreement, the state Caistab commodities board will hand farm-to-port price-setting for both coffee and cocoa to the private sector.
In addition, the private sector would in future make its own arrangements for auctioning export contracts -- currently managed by the Caistab.
"The auction will be private," said the source. The length of forward contracts could also be reduced, he added.
Ivory Coast sells two-thirds of each season's cocoa crop (Oct-Sept) on a forward basis before the season opens.
"Much of 1997/98 has already been sold," said the source.

Ivory Coast would present detailed privatisation plans for cocoa by mid-1998, taking into account partial coffee and cocoa liberalisation measures already in place and experiences in other countries, he said.
It would take into account a detailed coffee marketing study recently completed by British consultant Landell Mills.
Donors say the deal on coffee means Ivory Coast has now met the terms for an outstanding tranche of the $150 million World Bank Agriculture Sector Adjustment Credit (ASAC).
Cocoa reforms, included under the same package, would now be reviewed under the terms of a future ASAC agreement.
Terms for other sectors such as cotton and jute sack manufacturing sectors still had to be met.
Donors have also pushed for increases in reference cocoa and coffee prices in 1997/98, ahead of the reforms.
Caistab accounts show large financial reserves from cocoa exports and a positive account balance for coffee, despite plummeting world coffee prices in late 1996.
"I expect the prices will go up. They are working on the numbers," said one donor source.
Ivory Coast in late 1996 set a recommended 1996/97 farmgate price of 315 CFA a kilo for cocoa and 495 CFA a kilo for coffee.
Caistab and and governement officials were not available for comment on the talks with donors.
-- Matthew Bunce, Abidjan newsroom + 225 21 90 90
